items.title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
items.raw_text: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility. Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. items.title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
items.raw_text: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals. Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century. A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs , and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding. None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. items.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
items.raw_text: In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered: Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra [ ... ] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7. — Ted Sanders , explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions Tags: generative-ai , gpt , openai , ai , llms , ted-sanders

items.raw_text: Can the internet become a genuine public space rather than a collection of platforms dominated by commercial interests? This question opened the third day of MetLib 2026 , as keynote speaker Jantien Borsboom explored alternative models of digital public spaces and the role libraries could play in creating online environments that serve people rather than profit. The impact of artificial intelligence and the future of shared knowledge were also central themes. Erin Kissane addressed the challenges of maintaining public trust and collective understanding in an increasingly fragmented digital world. The day concluded with David Lankes , who invited participants to imagine librarianship in 2036, asking: Will librarians still focus primarily on collections and materials, or will they become community practitioners? His keynote challenged traditional definitions of the profession and highlighted the importance of flexibility of it. Throughout the day, discussions offered new perspectives on libraries — not merely as third places or community hubs, but as essential civic infrastructure , supporting democratic participation and social connections. items.raw_text: I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games . Tree Appreciator Emberwick Battle Drones Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove Four times as insulting What happens if someone actually puts the work in? You should build a game! Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game: 3D modeling Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox ) Game design (!) That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments . The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play . Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. items.raw_text: Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration. The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Health Again movement and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them. Kennedy said he uses some of the peptides and called himself a "big fan." But FDA scientists continue to say there is insufficient evidence to show if they're effective and they are potentially dangerous. In 2023, the safety concerns led the FDA to remove the six peptides from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies called compounding pharmacies—which make customized formulations of drugs for patients, or, in cases such as this, specialty drugs in bulk. Kennedy's new rule sidesteps the need to formally undo that FDA action. The rule is titled "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" and was made available Wednesday on the Federal Register , with the final publication data set for October 30. The rule does not change the regulatory status of the peptide; instead, it states the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will no longer take enforcement action against compounding pharmacies for making the peptides, essentially giving them a green light to freely produce and sell them. items.title: The last, best hope for space tourism just rolled onto a runway in Arizona
items.raw_text: The private space tourism era looked so very promising five years ago. Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic had begun flying customers—real people with zero space experience—on suborbital missions. And at about the same time, private citizens were going to orbit for days at a time aboard SpaceX's Crew Dragon. But that was then. Consider the state of play today: It has been 10 months since Blue Origin's New Shepard spacecraft flew its last mission in January. The program was subsequently "paused," but let's be real. Blue Origin has moved on. New Shepard's engineering teams are now supporting the New Glenn rocket and Blue Moon lander programs. SpaceX flew its final free-flyer mission on Dragon, Fram2, in April 2025. A handful of non-NASA missions bound for space stations remain on the spacecraft's manifest, but all are likely to carry at least one government astronaut. Then Dragon will be retired. There is no credible timeline for SpaceX's Starship to fly humans into space from Earth. As for Virgin Galactic, the company flew its final suborbital mission on the VSS Unity spacecraft more than two years ago, in June 2024. So we are now 10 months, and counting, without a space tourism mission in the United States. Read full article Comments

items.raw_text: The rapid decline of Antarctic sea ice since 2016 has triggered a dramatic shift in a crucial part of Earth’s climate system, scientists say. In a paper published Wednesday, researchers documented a sharp salinity increase in a vast layer of the Southern Ocean, extending from 2,300 to 4,000 feet deep and encircling Antarctica. The shift reverses decades of freshening and echoes ocean changes usually associated with major global climate shifts over millennia but is now happening in just a few years. The switch from a decades-long trend of freshening water to increasing salinity has implications that could extend beyond Antarctica. The layer, known as Antarctic Intermediate Water, spreads northward into the Indian, Pacific, and Atlantic oceans, transporting heat, carbon, oxygen, and nutrients toward the tropics, and even across the equator, said co-author Bishakhdatta Gayen , a researcher and professor at the University of Melbourne and at the Centre for Atmospheric and Oceanic Sciences in Bengaluru, India. Inside, engineers create the force behind our phones and computers and appliances, our streaming services and search engines and chatbots and vibe-coded apps and websites. Maar voor grote organisaties is afscheid nemen van Amerikaanse hyperscalers niet altijd nodig of realistisch. Cruciaal is keuzevrijheid op basis van een risicoanalyse: welke applicaties en gegevens kunnen bij hyperscalers blijven en welke moeten met prioriteit naar een soevereine cloud? De discussie over digitale soevereiniteit wordt nogal eens zwart-wit gevoerd. Amerikaanse technologie zou moeten worden vervangen door Europese alternatieven. items.title: Spoelstra Spreekt: Gaat niet gebeuren
items.raw_text: COLUMN – Gaan er ooit minder ambtenaren werken bij de overheid? Als je het mij vraagt, zeg ik: nee, alleen maar meer. Maar ja, niemand vraagt mij. Dit kabinet wil 25.000 minder ambtenaren. Dat staat in de voortgangsbrief Slagvaardige Overheid die staatssecretaris Eric van den Burg deze week naar de Tweede Kamer heeft gestuurd. Dat het kabinet en de Tweede Kamer nog steeds met brieven communiceren, zegt al dat er nog wel een paar stappen in de automatisering te zetten zijn. De staatssecretaris is vergeten zich in te lezen in de geschiedenis van automatisering bij de overheid Het had ook gewoon met een appje gekund. ‘Joh, we gaan verder met 25.000 ambtenaren minder 😊👍’. Scheelt meteen een voortgangsbrief. En waarschijnlijk drie beleidsmedewerkers die hem schrijven, twee communicatiemedewerkers die hem redigeren en een woordvoerder die uitlegt wat er eigenlijk in staat. Vervangen Het kabinet denkt de reductie van ambtenaren te realiseren door hun werk te vervangen door ai . Ik denk dat de staatssecretaris vergeten is zich in te lezen in de geschiedenis van automatisering bij de overheid. Automatisering bij de overheid betekent dat er niet minder, maar juist véél meer mensen komen te werken. Meestal betekent het dat er eerst een projectgroep komt die gaat onderzoeken hoe automatisering ervoor kan zorgen dat er minder mensen komen te werken. Die projectgroep heeft een programmamanager nodig. En een projectleider. En iemand van informatievoorziening. En iemand van juridische zaken.
